solution:
The mean square speed INCREASES, in direct proportion to the ABSOLUTE temperature.

From the kinetic interpretation of temperature, the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is

\( \dfrac{1}{2} m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T \)

\( \therefore \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{3 k_{B} T}{m} \), i.e. \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \propto T \) for a given gas.

So if the absolute temperature is doubled, the mean square speed \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \) is doubled, while the root mean square speed \( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}}} \) grows only by a factor \( \sqrt{2} \) — the two are different quantities and the proportionality quoted here is for the MEAN SQUARE speed.

Two cautions. \( T \) must be in kelvin: raising the temperature from \( 27\ ^\circ \text{C} \) to \( 54\ ^\circ \text{C} \) does not double \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \), because in kelvin those are 300 K and 327 K, a rise of only 9%. And the proportionality is per gas — at the same \( T \) a heavier molecule has a smaller \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \), since \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \propto 1/m \).

The number of degrees of freedom (dof) of a molecule depends on:

1. **The number of atoms in the molecule.** A monatomic molecule (He, Ar) has only the 3 translational dof of its centre of mass, so \( f = 3 \). A diatomic molecule (\( \mathrm{O}_{2} \), \( \mathrm{N}_{2} \), CO) adds 2 rotational dof about the two axes perpendicular to the internuclear axis, giving \( f = 5 \).

2. **The geometry (arrangement) of the atoms.** Rotation about an axis along which the atoms lie does not change the positions of the atoms and so is not counted — this is why a diatomic molecule gets 2 rotational dof and not 3, while a non-linear polyatomic molecule gets all 3.

3. **The constraints on the molecule's motion — the dimensionality in which it is free to move.** A molecule free to move in three-dimensional space has 3 translational dof; one restricted to a plane has 2; one restricted to a straight line has 1.

4. **The temperature.** The vibrational modes are frozen out at ordinary temperatures and become active only at high temperature. Each vibrational mode contributes TWO quadratic terms (one kinetic, one potential), so a non-rigid diatomic molecule at high temperature has \( f = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 \).

In general the degrees of freedom are the total number of independent coordinates or quantities needed to describe the position and configuration of the system completely.

The ideal gas equation for \( n \) moles is \( PV = nRT \).

Nitrogen is diatomic, \( \mathrm{N}_{2} \), so its molar mass is \( M_{0} = 2 \times 14 = 28 \) g \( \text{mol}^{-1} \).

Number of moles in 7 g:

\( n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_{0}} = \dfrac{7 \text{ g}}{28 \text{ g mol}^{-1}} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25 \text{ mol} \)

Hence for 7 g of nitrogen gas

\( PV = \dfrac{1}{4} R T \), i.e. \( PV = \dfrac{RT}{4} \)

with \( P \) in \( \text{N m}^{-2} \), \( V \) in \( \text{m}^{3} \), \( T \) in kelvin and \( R = 8.31 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \).

(Note that the molar mass to use is 28, that of the \( \mathrm{N}_{2} \) MOLECULE, not 14, that of the nitrogen atom.)

**Ideal gas.** A gas that obeys the ideal gas equation \( PV = nRT \) at ALL pressures and ALL temperatures is called an ideal gas. In an ideal gas the intermolecular interactions are absent: the molecules are treated as point particles of negligible size which exert no force on one another except during the brief, perfectly elastic collisions. Consequently an ideal gas has no intermolecular potential energy and its internal energy is purely kinetic.

**Does it exist in practice? No.** Real gases are composed of atoms or molecules that do have a finite size and that do interact with one another, so no real gas is truly ideal.

What is true in practice is that a real gas APPROACHES ideal behaviour when its molecules are far enough apart for the interactions to be negligible — that is, at sufficiently low density: at low pressure and at high temperature, with the temperature well above the gas's liquefaction temperature. Under those conditions the ideal gas equation describes a real gas closely, which is why the ideal gas serves as a useful model.

Of the thermal radiation incident on a body, the fractions absorbed, reflected and transmitted satisfy \( a + r + t_{\mathrm{r}} = 1 \). The two terms below classify a substance by its coefficient of transmission \( t_{\mathrm{r}} \).

**Diathermanous substances:** substances through which heat radiations can pass, i.e. for which \( t_{\mathrm{r}} \neq 0 \). A diathermanous body is neither a good absorber nor a good reflector.
Examples: glass, quartz, sodium chloride, hydrogen, oxygen, dry air.

**Athermanous substances:** substances which are largely opaque to thermal radiation, i.e. which do NOT transmit the heat radiation incident on them, so \( t_{\mathrm{r}} = 0 \) and \( a + r = 1 \).
Examples: water, wood, iron, copper, moist air, benzene.

One caution the chapter makes explicitly: \( a \), \( r \) and \( t_{\mathrm{r}} \) depend on the WAVELENGTH of the incident radiation as well as on the material, so the same object can be diathermanous for one range of wavelengths and athermanous for another.

On the kinetic theory, the temperature of a gas is nothing but a measure of the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules. From the interpretation of temperature,

\( \dfrac{1}{2} m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T \), i.e. \( T = \dfrac{m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}}}{3 k_{B}} \)

so the absolute temperature is DEFINED, kinetically, by the average kinetic energy per molecule.

When the gas is heated, the heat supplied is transferred to the randomly moving molecules and appears as an increase in their kinetic energy — in an ideal gas there is no intermolecular potential energy, so every joule supplied must go into molecular kinetic energy. The mean square speed \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \) therefore rises, the average kinetic energy per molecule \( \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T \) rises with it, and this is exactly what we register on a thermometer as a rise in temperature.

The molecules also now move faster, so they strike the walls more often and with greater momentum. That is the microscopic reason the pressure of a gas heated at constant volume also increases.

In short: heating raises the average molecular kinetic energy, and the absolute temperature IS that average kinetic energy in disguise — hence the temperature increases.

The pressure INCREASES — in inverse proportion to the volume.

From the kinetic theory, the pressure exerted by an ideal gas is

\( P = \dfrac{1}{3} \dfrac{N}{V} m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \)

where \( N/V \) is the number of molecules per unit volume and \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \) is the mean square speed.

The process is at CONSTANT TEMPERATURE, and \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = 3 k_{B} T / m \) depends only on the temperature. So the molecular speeds are unchanged; the only quantity that changes is the number density.

When the volume \( V \) is reduced, the same \( N \) molecules are confined in a smaller space, so \( N/V \) increases. The molecules therefore have a shorter distance to travel between one wall collision and the next, and strike unit area of the wall MORE OFTEN in a given time. Each impact still delivers the same average momentum (the speeds have not changed), but there are more impacts per second per unit area, so the rate of momentum transfer to unit area — which is the pressure — goes up.

Since \( m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \) and \( N \) are fixed, \( P \propto \dfrac{1}{V} \), so halving the volume doubles the pressure. This is precisely Boyle's law, here obtained from the molecular picture.

A real gas obeys the ideal gas equation \( PV = nRT \) only when its molecules are so far apart that the two ways in which a real gas departs from the ideal model — the finite size of the molecules and the forces between them — both become negligible. The conditions are:

1. **Low pressure.** At low pressure the molecules are widely separated, so the volume actually occupied by the molecules themselves is negligible compared with the volume of the container.

2. **High temperature.** At high temperature the molecules move fast and their kinetic energy is large compared with the intermolecular potential energy, so the intermolecular attractions have negligible effect during the brief encounters.

3. **Low density**, which is the condition the first two together produce: the gas must be sufficiently rarefied for there to be practically no interatomic or intermolecular interaction.

4. **Temperature well above the liquefaction (condensation) temperature of the gas**, so that the gas is nowhere near the region in which attractive forces cause it to condense.

Under these conditions the real gas is said to be in the *ideal state* and its behaviour is close to that of an ideal gas. Conversely, the deviations are largest at HIGH pressure and LOW temperature.

**Law of equipartition of energy.** For a gas in thermal equilibrium at a temperature \( T \), the average energy per molecule associated with each quadratic term in its energy — that is, with each degree of freedom — is \( \dfrac{1}{2} k_{B} T \). Equivalently, the total energy is shared equally among all the degrees of freedom.

For one MOLE, multiply by Avogadro's number \( N_{A} \) and use \( N_{A} k_{B} = R \): each degree of freedom contributes \( \dfrac{1}{2} R T \) per mole. So for a gas whose molecule has \( f \) degrees of freedom,

\( E = \dfrac{f}{2} R T \), \( \quad C_{V} = \dfrac{dE}{dT} = \dfrac{f}{2} R \), \( \quad C_{P} = C_{V} + R = \left( \dfrac{f}{2} + 1 \right) R \)

the second of which is Mayer's relation \( C_{P} - C_{V} = R \).

**(a) Monatomic gas** (He, Ar, Ne — a single atom, so translation only): \( f = 3 \).

\( C_{V} = \dfrac{3}{2} R = 1.5 \times 8.31 = 12.47 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \)

\( C_{P} = \dfrac{5}{2} R = 2.5 \times 8.31 = 20.78 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \)

\( \gamma = \dfrac{C_{P}}{C_{V}} = \dfrac{5}{3} = 1.67 \)

**(b) Diatomic gas** (\( \mathrm{O}_{2} \), \( \mathrm{N}_{2} \), CO) **treated as a rigid rotator**, which is the case at ordinary temperatures: 3 translational + 2 rotational dof, so \( f = 5 \).

\( C_{V} = \dfrac{5}{2} R = 20.78 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \)

\( C_{P} = \dfrac{7}{2} R = 29.09 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \)

\( \gamma = \dfrac{7}{5} = 1.40 \)

**(c) Diatomic gas at high temperature**, when the vibrational mode becomes active. A vibration contributes TWO quadratic terms, one kinetic and one potential, so \( f = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 \).

\( C_{V} = \dfrac{7}{2} R = 29.09 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \), \( \quad C_{P} = \dfrac{9}{2} R = 37.40 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \), \( \quad \gamma = \dfrac{9}{7} = 1.29 \)

Note that the answer for a diatomic gas is not unique until the molecule is specified as rigid or non-rigid — hence the value of \( f \) must always be stated with the result.

**(i) Stefan-Boltzmann law.** The rate of emission of radiant energy per unit area of a perfect blackbody (its emissive power) is directly proportional to the FOURTH power of its ABSOLUTE temperature.

\( R \propto T^{4} \), i.e. \( R = \sigma T^{4} \)

where \( \sigma \) is Stefan's constant, \( \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \) J \( \text{m}^{-2} \text{s}^{-1} \text{K}^{-4} \) (equivalently W \( \text{m}^{-2} \text{K}^{-4} \)).

For a body of surface area \( A \) and emissivity \( e \) the rate of emission is \( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = e \sigma A T^{4} \), and if the body is placed in surroundings at temperature \( T_{0} \) the NET rate of loss of heat is

\( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = e \sigma A \left( T^{4} - T_{0}^{4} \right) \)

**(ii) Wien's displacement law.** The wavelength \( \lambda_{\max} \) at which the emissive power of a blackbody is a maximum is inversely proportional to its ABSOLUTE temperature.

\( \lambda_{\max} \propto \dfrac{1}{T} \), i.e. \( \lambda_{\max} T = b \)

where \( b \) is Wien's constant, \( b = 2.897 \times 10^{-3} \) m K.

So the hotter the body, the shorter the wavelength at which it dominantly radiates — the peak of the spectral distribution curve is displaced towards the shorter-wavelength (blue) end as the temperature rises. This is what lets us estimate the surface temperatures of the Sun and of distant stars.

In both laws \( T \) must be in KELVIN; using a Celsius value makes both statements false.

The radiant energy emitted per unit area per unit time by a blackbody is not distributed uniformly over wavelength. If \( R_{\lambda} \), the radiant power per unit area per unit wavelength range, is plotted against \( \lambda \) for a body held at a fixed temperature, a continuous single-peaked curve is obtained; a family of such curves at different temperatures is the spectral distribution of blackbody radiation. Lummer and Pringsheim measured these curves experimentally, keeping a cavity radiator at different constant temperatures.

The experimental curves show that:

1. At a given temperature the energy is NOT uniformly distributed over the spectrum.

2. At a given temperature the radiant power starts at zero, increases with wavelength, reaches a maximum at a wavelength \( \lambda_{\max} \), and then decreases, tailing off asymptotically. \( \lambda_{\max} \) is characteristic of the TEMPERATURE of the body — it is not the maximum wavelength emitted, but the wavelength of maximum intensity.

3. The AREA under a curve represents the total energy emitted per unit time per unit area at all wavelengths, i.e. \( \sigma T^{4} \) (Stefan-Boltzmann law).

4. As the temperature rises the peak shifts LEFT, towards shorter wavelengths: \( \lambda_{\max} \) decreases as \( T \) increases, which is Wien's displacement law \( \lambda_{\max} T = b \).

5. At higher temperature the radiant power at EVERY wavelength is greater, so the whole curve lies above the curves for lower temperatures and the area under it (the total emission) increases rapidly, as \( T^{4} \). Consequently two curves for different temperatures never cross.

6. At about 300 K (room temperature) practically all the radiant energy is carried by waves longer than those of red light — that is, in the infrared.

The distribution depends only on the absolute temperature of the blackbody and not on the material of which it is made. Classical theory could not explain the curves: Wien's expression fitted only the short-wavelength end, while the Rayleigh-Jeans formula, obtained from the equipartition of energy, fitted the long-wavelength end but tended to infinity at short wavelengths. Planck's quantum hypothesis — that the oscillators exchange energy only in discrete quanta \( E = nh\nu \) — reproduced the observed spectrum over the whole range.

**Statement.** At a given temperature, the ratio of the emissive power to the coefficient of absorption of a body is equal to the emissive power of a perfect blackbody at the same temperature, for all wavelengths.

\( \dfrac{R}{a} = R_{B} \)

Equivalently, since the emissivity is defined as \( e = R / R_{B} \), the law states that for a body emitting and absorbing thermal radiation in thermal equilibrium, the emissivity equals the absorptivity:

\( a = e \), or more specifically \( a(\lambda) = e(\lambda) \)

So a good absorber is a good emitter and a poor absorber is a poor emitter.

**Theoretical proof.** Consider an ordinary body A and a perfect blackbody B of identical geometrical shape, placed in an enclosure. In thermal equilibrium both bodies are at the same temperature as the enclosure, and neither is heating up or cooling down.

Let \( R \) be the emissive power of A, \( R_{B} \) that of the blackbody B, and \( a \) the coefficient of absorption of A. Let \( Q \) be the quantity of radiant heat incident on each body per unit area per unit time.

Body A absorbs only the fraction \( a \) of what falls on it:

quantity absorbed by A \( = Q_{a} = a Q \)

Since the temperature of A stays constant, it must emit in unit time exactly what it absorbs in unit time:

quantity emitted by A \( = \) quantity absorbed by A

\( \therefore R = a Q \) ... (1)

Apply the same argument to the perfect blackbody B. It absorbs ALL the incident radiation, since \( a_{B} = 1 \), and being also in equilibrium it emits as much as it absorbs:

\( \therefore R_{B} = Q \) ... (2)

Dividing (1) by (2),

\( \dfrac{R}{R_{B}} = a \), that is \( \dfrac{R}{a} = R_{B} \)

But by definition \( \dfrac{R}{R_{B}} = e \), the emissivity of A.

\( \therefore a = e \)

which is Kirchhoff's law, proved.

**Everyday consequences.** The bottoms of cooking utensils are blackened so that they absorb (and emit) well, while their tops are polished so that they neither absorb nor radiate much; and the walls of a thermos flask are silvered because a good reflector is a poor absorber and hence also a poor emitter, which suppresses heat exchange by radiation.
